intro: This guide takes your group through How to Succeed in the Christian Life (For Teens) in twelve weeks, one chapter each week. It’s written for teenagers aged about 13 to 18 and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. R. A. Torrey wrote the book for new Christians who wanted to know how to keep going, and this edition passes on his practical advice: beginning right by receiving Jesus, confessing him openly, assurance, the Holy Spirit, Bible reading, prayer, friendships, sharing faith, standing firm and taking the next step. It is especially useful for teens who have just come to faith or want to grow.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Welcome everyone and say the memory verse together. Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand. Talk it through using the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you. Do the activity, which takes about 10 minutes. Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper, pens and Bibles. Chapter 1 tells how Torrey, as a student, was so full of despair that he meant to end his life, so read it ahead, handle it gently, and know where to point a teen for help, including a crisis line where you live. Other chapters touch on doubts about salvation, guilt, hard questions about the Bible and being mocked or bullied for faith; make room for honest questions, keep personal reflection private, and follow up quietly with anyone who seems anxious or is being hurt. Where Christians describe the Holy Spirit’s work differently, Chapter 5 leaves room for your church’s own teaching.

weeks.summary: R. A. Torrey, born in 1856 to a wealthy family and prayed for by his mother, threw himself into the theatre, horse racing, card games and heavy drinking at Yale until one night in 1875 he was in such despair that he meant to end his life, but prayed instead and promised to do whatever God asked. He became a minister, trusted God for his family’s needs, led Moody’s Bible school, was known for prayer and preached around the world. He wrote this book for new Christians. The big idea: it is never too late to begin again with God.

memory_verse.text: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it.

activity.title: Begin Again
steps: Read aloud Torrey’s line: “If any one who reads these pages has begun wrong, it is a very simple matter to begin over again and begin right.”
Discuss the part his mother’s prayers played in his story.
Ask everyone to write down, for themselves, one area of life where they would like to begin again with God.
Invite each person to think of someone who has prayed for them and plan how to thank them this week.
Close by reminding the group that if anyone ever feels as low as Torrey did, they should tell a trusted adult straight away, and that you are available to talk.

weeks.summary: Torrey says nothing matters more than beginning right, and the right beginning is receiving Jesus: taking him to be for yourself all that God offers him to be, the one who died for your sins and your risen Lord. Nobody is too bad to receive him, and nobody is too good to need to. Growing up in church or being nice is not the same as personally receiving him. The big idea: the Christian life begins by receiving Jesus, and anyone can begin right today.

memory_verse.text: But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God.

activity.title: Knowing About or Receiving?
steps: Draw two columns on a board: “Knowing about Jesus” and “Receiving Jesus.”
Ask the group to suggest what belongs in each column, using the chapter.
Discuss Torrey’s two points: nobody is too bad, and nobody is too good.
Read John 1:12 and John 3:16 aloud together.
Give everyone a quiet minute to talk to Jesus privately, either receiving him for the first time or thanking him for making them God’s child.

weeks.summary: Torrey says a secret disciple is no disciple at all: when Jesus is real to us it shows, and we should confess him constantly at home, at school and at play, without parading our faith. He warns that failing to confess Christ is a common cause of drifting away, while letting it be known protects us from temptation. The big idea: don’t show off, but don’t hide; the more you make of Jesus, the more he will make of you.

memory_verse.text: So everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven.

activity.title: Natural, Not Pushy
steps: Read Torrey’s line: “we should not parade our Christianity or our piety, but we should leave no one in doubt whether we belong to Christ.”
As a group, list everyday moments when a teen might naturally let people know they follow Jesus, such as being asked about the weekend.
Sort the ideas into “natural” and “showing off,” and discuss the difference.
Talk about how being known as a Christian can protect someone from pressure.
Challenge everyone to try one natural way of letting someone know they follow Jesus this week.

weeks.summary: Torrey teaches from 1 John 5:13 that Christians can know they have eternal life, not because of changing feelings but because God’s word says so. This assurance brings joy and power, and when the enemy brings up our past sins, we should look at what God looks at: Jesus on the cross. Brooding over forgiven sins, Torrey says, is ingratitude, not humility. The big idea: if you have received Jesus, you can know you belong to God, because God has said so.

memory_verse.text: I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God that you may know that you have eternal life.

activity.title: Feelings or Facts?
steps: Draw a wavy line on a board labelled “feelings” and a straight line labelled “God’s promises.”
Discuss what kinds of things make our feelings about God go up and down.
Read Torrey’s words about brooding over sins God has cancelled, and talk about why that is not true humility.
Give everyone a card to write out 1 John 5:13 and John 1:12.
Encourage them to read the card whenever they feel unsure this week and say: “God says I can know. I trust what he says.”

weeks.summary: Torrey tells how Paul met twelve disciples in Ephesus who had not heard of the Holy Spirit, and after the Spirit came on them a great revival followed. He calls receiving the Spirit the secret of joy, victory over sin, power in prayer and effective service, while noting every Christian has the Spirit in some sense. Christians describe this differently, but all agree the Christian life is not lived in our own strength. The big idea: ask God honestly for the Holy Spirit, and trust him to give.

memory_verse.text: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.

activity.title: Ask, Don’t Fake It
steps: Read Acts 19:1–6 aloud together.
Then read Luke 11:11–13 and discuss what Jesus says about the Father’s willingness to give.
Talk about the four things Torrey says the Spirit brings: joy, victory over sin, power in prayer and effective service. Which do teens most want?
Discuss why we don’t need to fake an experience or work up emotions.
Encourage everyone to pray each morning this week: “Father, you promised to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. I’m asking. Fill me today.”

weeks.summary: Torrey’s secret of joy and victory is never to lose sight of Jesus: look at him on the cross when you feel guilty, look at him risen when you are tempted, and follow him in everything. He warns that one of the commonest causes of failure is following a good person we admire, because no one, however good, can be safely followed. The big idea: build your faith on Jesus, not on Christian heroes, and keep looking at him.

memory_verse.text: Looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.

activity.title: Three Ways to Look
steps: Write three situations on a board: “I feel guilty,” “I’m tempted” and “I don’t know what to do.”
Ask the group to match each one with Torrey’s three ways of looking at Jesus: on the cross, risen, and as the one we follow.
Discuss why following a Christian hero can be risky, and what happens when a hero lets us down.
Ask everyone to write down, for themselves, which of the three situations they meet most often.
Encourage them to practise that way of looking at Jesus each time it comes up this week.

weeks.summary: Torrey says nothing matters more for spiritual growth than regular, systematic Bible study. The Bible is the soul’s food, a weekly sermon is not enough, and we must learn to feed ourselves, never letting a day pass without reading. Even after twenty-five years as a Christian he would not dare to skip a day. The big idea: a little of God’s word every day is far better than a lot once in a while.

memory_verse.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.

activity.title: A Chapter a Day
steps: Read Torrey’s comparison between food for the body and food for the soul.
Have everyone read Mark 1 or John 1 quietly to themselves.
Ask each person to write down one verse that stood out, and what it shows about God, about themselves, and what to do.
Share a few of the verses as a group, for those who wish.
Challenge everyone to read one chapter every day this week and write down a verse from each.

weeks.summary: Torrey admits the Bible has hard parts and wants them faced honestly. Difficulties are to be expected in a revelation from an infinite God, a difficulty doesn’t prove something false, as the phases of Venus later showed astronomers, and there are bigger difficulties in thinking the Bible merely human. His advice: be honest, keep reading, ask questions and don’t give up what you have good reason to trust. The big idea: you don’t need every answer to keep following Jesus.

memory_verse.text: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.

activity.title: Question Box
activity.materials: Slips of paper, pens and a box or bag
steps: Give everyone a slip of paper to write down, anonymously, one hard question about the Bible or faith.
Collect the slips in a box or bag and mix them up.
Read a few out and talk about them together, using Torrey’s points that difficulties are expected and don’t prove something false.
Note any questions you can’t answer now and promise to come back to them.
Encourage everyone to ask a wise Christian adult about their own question this week.

weeks.summary: Torrey, famous for prayer, says anyone who wants to succeed as a Christian must lead a life of prayer, with set times alone with God as well as praying anywhere. Prayer is a privilege, an audience with the King and talking with our Father. His practical tip is to start the day with thanks and to pray ahead about the day’s temptations, as Jesus prayed in Gethsemane while the disciples slept. The big idea: win your battles on your knees before temptation comes.

memory_verse.text: Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan, and he hears my voice.

activity.title: Plan the Day in Prayer
steps: Read Torrey’s words: “Anticipate your battles, fight them on your knees before temptation comes and you will always have victory.”
Ask everyone to write down, for themselves, a typical tomorrow, from waking to bedtime.
Have them mark two or three moments where they expect something hard: a lesson, a person or a temptation.
Spend a few minutes in quiet prayer over those moments, starting with thanks.
Challenge everyone to take five minutes each morning this week to do the same before leaving the house.

weeks.summary: Torrey says our companions shape our character, and encourages every young Christian to have a few close Christian friends to talk and pray with. We should also know people who don’t share our faith, always seeking to lift them up, and give up a friendship that keeps dragging us from God. On fun, he says young people need recreation and offers questions rather than rules: can I do it to God’s glory, take Christ with me and ask his blessing on it? The big idea: choose friends and fun that help you grow, as a trusting, glad child of God.

memory_verse.text: Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm.

activity.title: Torrey’s Questions
steps: Write Torrey’s questions on a board: Can I do this to the glory of God? Will it hurt my influence for good? Can I pray about it and ask God’s blessing? Can I take Christ with me there?
Read out a few made-up situations, such as a party invitation, a new game, a film or an app.
In small groups, have teens run each situation through the questions and decide what they would do.
Discuss the difference between using the questions wisely and becoming anxious about everything.
Ask everyone to think privately about the three or four people they spend most time with, and thank God for the good friends among them.

weeks.summary: Torrey says the working Christian is the happy and strong Christian: serving God keeps the soul healthy, and those busy winning others to Christ are full of joy. For teens that might mean praying for friends, inviting someone along or being honest about faith. He also had a heart for missions, saying some can go, all can give and all can pray. The big idea: following Jesus means helping others know him, starting where you are.

memory_verse.text: And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.”

activity.title: Three Names
steps: Read Torrey’s line: “The working Christian is the happy Christian. The working Christian is the strong Christian.”
As a group, list realistic ways a teenager can help others know Jesus, from prayer to kindness to an invitation.
Give everyone a card to write down, privately, the first names of three friends who don’t yet know Jesus.
Talk about Torrey’s three ways to “go”: go, give and pray, and which ones the group could do now.
Encourage everyone to pray for their three friends by name every day this week.

weeks.summary: Torrey warns that following Jesus will bring some opposition, which can help rather than hinder if received rightly, but we must make sure it is for Jesus’ sake and not because we are stubborn or unkind: never yield principle, and do it in love. His final chapter is about guidance: admit you need wisdom, surrender your will, ask, expect an answer and follow step by step, because all you need to know is the next step. The big idea: stand firm in love, and trust God for the next step.

memory_verse.text: Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.

activity.title: The Next Step
steps: Read Torrey’s story of the worried student and his words, “All you need to know is the next step.”
Discuss the difference between being opposed for Jesus’ sake and being disliked for being stubborn or unkind.
Remind the group that bullying or threats, for faith or anything else, should never be carried alone, and that they can tell you or another trusted adult.
Ask everyone to write down, for themselves, what they already know God wants them to do this week.
Look back together over the whole book and invite each person to name one habit they want to keep.
